articles.title: Stranded for 11 months, no wages for 5: 7 Indian seafarers repatriated from Abu Dhabi tanker
articles.summary: India News: Seven Indian seafarers allegedly stranded aboard the oil products tanker MV Sea Star 2 at Mina Zayed Port in Abu Dhabi for 11 months have been repatri.
articles.body: Seven Indian seafarers allegedly stranded aboard the oil products tanker MV Sea Star 2 at Mina Zayed Port in Abu Dhabi for 11 months have been repatriated, while efforts are under way to bring home the remaining crew members.In a post on X, the Embassy said it "is closely following up with local authorities on the welfare and early repatriation of Indian seafarers stranded aboard SEA STAR 2. Seven seafarers have already been repatriated, and efforts are underway for the safe and early repatriation of the remaining seafarers."According to FSUI, the remaining seafarers have not received wages for five months. The union also alleged that the vessel's owner deducted visa and travel expenses from earlier payments and that important travel documents remain under the control of port authorities.FSUI had urged the ministry of external affairs, Directorate General of Shipping, Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and International Transport Workers' Federation to intervene, demanding payment of the outstanding wages and immediate repatriation of the crew. India steps up focus on seafarer safetyThe development comes amid heightened concerns over the safety of Indian seafarers operating in waters affected by the Iran conflict. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal recently said the "welfare and safety of India's seafaring community remains a high priority" and that New Delhi raises such issues with relevant authorities whenever they arise.His comments followed the release of footage by FSUI alleging that Iranian naval forces had harassed a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz on April 22.According to the union, the Panama-flagged vessel was carrying 22 crew members, including 21 Indians, when it was surrounded by small armed boats. FSUI alleged that the boats belonged to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy and that an RPG was fired at the vessel, forcing crew members to take shelter inside the ship.FSUI has used the incident to call for "direct naval escorts and stronger physical protection" for Indian seafarers operating in high-risk maritime zones.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Nimaya Williams, the North Carolina junior who completed free college-planning steps and became one of only two students nationwide to receive a $40,000 BigFuture scholarship
articles.summary: US News: For many high-school students, preparing for life after graduation can feel overwhelming. College applications, career choices, financial planning, an.
articles.body: For many high-school students, preparing for life after graduation can feel overwhelming. College applications, career choices, financial planning, and scholarship searches can all seem like separate challenges, especially for students who are still figuring out what they want their future to look like. For Nimaya Williams, a junior at Westover High School in Fayetteville, North Carolina, taking practical steps toward that future recently brought an unexpected reward: a $40,000 scholarship that could help change the course of her college journey. Williams was selected by College Board's BigFuture as one of only two students nationwide to receive the monthly $40,000 BigFuture Scholarship, according to a July 2026 news release from Cumberland County Schools. She earned the award by completing college and career planning activities through BigFuture, College Board's free online platform.A surprise worth $40,000Williams did not expect her college-planning efforts to result in such a major award. When she received the surprise announcement, the Westover High School junior was overcome with emotion. âIâm about to cry. This is life changing,â Williams said in the Cumberland County Schools release, adding that she felt she was âdestined to do great things.âThe recognition came as Williams worked through the steps offered by BigFuture, a platform designed to help students prepare for life after high school. Rather than requiring students to win an academic competition or submit a traditional scholarship essay, the programme rewards eligible students for taking proactive steps toward college and career planning. For Williams, those actions ultimately led to one of the programme's largest monthly awards.Turning planning into opportunityThe BigFuture Scholarship is connected to activities that encourage students to think seriously about their futures. BigFuture helps students explore potential careers, prepare for college, and find ways to finance higher education. Williams' story highlights that college preparation does not necessarily begin with filling out an application. It can start much earlier, with students exploring career interests, learning about colleges, and thinking about how they will finance their education.That approach can be particularly important for high-school students who may not yet have a detailed plan for what comes after graduation. Taking smaller steps can help make a complicated process more manageable. Williams' scholarship also demonstrates how planning can sometimes open unexpected doors for students.A major relief for her familyThe $40,000 award could have an impact beyond Williams herself. Her mother, Shantay Dupree, said the scholarship would create more opportunities for her daughter while easing some of the financial pressure surrounding college. Dupree said Williams has many strengths and described the scholarship as an important step toward her future. She also acknowledged that paying for college can be difficult for families when money is tight.For families facing the rising cost of higher education, a scholarship of this size can make a meaningful difference. It can reduce the amount the student and family need to cover through savings, loans, or other financial assistance. The award therefore represents more than a moment of recognition for Williams. It could provide additional flexibility as she prepares for college.No essay or GPA requirementOne notable aspect of the BigFuture Scholarship programme is that students do not have to meet traditional academic requirements to be eligible. According to Cumberland County Schools, the programme does not require an essay, test score, GPA, or family-income qualification.The programme awards both $500 and $40,000 scholarships to eligible students attending two- or four-year colleges. The programme awards two $40,000 scholarships and hundreds of $500 scholarships each month. Since the programme began in 2019, BigFuture has awarded more than $25 million in scholarships to more than 30,000 students who took proactive steps toward their futures, according to the school district's announcement. That makes Williams' achievement part of a broader effort to encourage students to begin preparing for college and careers before graduation.A step toward her futureWilliams' story shows that preparing for college does not always have to mean accomplishing something extraordinary overnight. Sometimes, it begins with completing one planning activity, exploring a career, or learning more about financing education. Her decision to take those steps through BigFuture ultimately brought an unexpected $40,000 opportunity.For Williams and her family, the scholarship arrives at an important point in her high-school journey. With another year before graduation, she now has additional financial support as she considers what comes next. What started as a practical effort to plan for college has turned into a significant milestone, one that could help Williams move toward the future she already believes she is destined to achieve.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The RSF’s defeat will not end Sudan’s war but merely fragment it
articles.summary: Sudanese army’s battlefield gains rely on an armed coalition it may struggle to control once the common enemy is gone.
articles.body:
Sudan’s army has had a good summer. Last month, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) recaptured several towns along the strategic Export Road, known locally as Sadirat, which connects the central Nile valley to the country’s west, and pushed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) into a defensive crouch across much of the centre of the country.

On the back of these gains, SAF leaders are now speaking more confidently of defeating the RSF entirely, rather than merely containing it.

But look east, to Sudan’s Blue Nile state, and the picture inverts. In mid-August, the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (led by Abdulaziz al-Hilu), retook Kurmuk and seized Geisan within days, in attacks that Sudanese military sources said were launched from across the border in Ethiopia. Drone attacks on multiple army-controlled cities this month also showed that the RSF’s reach extends well beyond Darfur, its main territorial stronghold.

The lesson of the summer, then, is not that the SAF is on the verge of decisive victory. It is that military victory and political resolution are becoming two very different things. Even a full RSF defeat may not end Sudan’s war so much as fracture it into several smaller conflicts.

A look at the coalitions doing the fighting helps explain why. The anti-RSF coalition is coordinated and led by the SAF, but the army also relies on allied armed movements, including Darfuri factions that signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement (JPA). These include Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim’s Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) and the Sudan Liberation Movement, led by Darfur Governor Minni Minnawi. The JPA required their forces to be integrated into Sudan’s military and security services, but they have been reluctant to give up the military autonomy that underpins their political leverage.

Yasser al-Atta, then assistant commander-in-chief and now army chief of staff, announced in March that the army would activate mechanisms to organise and integrate allied irregular groups into the formal military and security services, but little has happened since.

Al-Atta wasn’t even the first to promise to address the problems of the proliferation of weapons and armed groups. Two years earlier, deputy commander-in-chief Shams al-Din Kabbashi told a graduation ceremony for Minni Minnawi’s Sudan Liberation Movement fighters that the army had “begun enacting a law and structures to control the many popular resistance groups”, warning that the array of semi-autonomous militias, tribal coalitions and volunteers backing the SAF’s war efforts, the “popular resistance” as it is called, would “become the next danger if we continue this way”.

More than two years on from Kabbashi’s speech, the underlying problem remains largely unresolved.

Then there is the RSF’s own coalition, which is actively fragmenting. A string of senior figures, al-Nour al-Qubba, al-Savanna, and more recently, the RSF-appointed governor for the Kordofan region, Hamad Khalifa, have defected, amid reports of Saudi financial inducements as well as tribal grievances.

When al-Nour al-Qubba left, he took dozens of combat vehicles and a large contingent of fighters with him. Given that the RSF is a franchise more than a unified fighting force, these defections should worry the SAF as much as they comfort it: defectors often arrive as intact forces loyal to their commanders, not soldiers used to reporting to a chain of command. In a way, the SAF inherits the RSF’s structural weakness with each defection.

Another example is Abu Aqla Keikel, an SAF-trained officer who initially fought on the army’s side after the war erupted in 2023, before defecting to the RSF later that year and then back to the SAF in October 2024. His Sudan Shield Forces remain, in practice, more under his own command than the army’s, even as he appears alongside SAF leadership and Darfuri commanders at recent battlefield-victory photo ops.

Many commanders inside the anti-RSF camp maintain a fairly wide margin of operational independence and consequently their own political calculations. This will become far more apparent once the war ends and there is no longer a common enemy to paper over the differences.

Sudan’s Islamists, meanwhile, occupy a strange position. Brigades like al-Baraa ibn Malik, affiliated with Sudan’s Islamic Movement, which underpinned Omar al-Bashir’s former ruling National Congress Party (NCP), supplied thousands of fighters and were instrumental in retaking Khartoum from the RSF. The United States has sanctioned al-Baraa ibn Malik, while the European Union has sanctioned its leader, al-Misbah Abu Zaid. Amid this international pressure and SAF battlefield gains, some Islamist fighters and leaders have begun pulling back, in what one Sudan Tribune report described as a “tactical withdrawal”. Al-Misbah recently posted that “we have returned to our civilian lives”.

But retreating from the battlefield is not the same as retreating from politics. Ahmed Haroun, chairman of the former ruling NCP, told Reuters news agency last year that the Islamic Movement could support an extended period of army rule, with an eye towards returning to government through “the ballot box”, as Haroun put it.

Indeed, another potential flashpoint for the SAF is that the war has given fighters in Islamist brigades like al-Baraa ibn Malik years of battlefield experience. There is little reason to think fighters who helped recapture the capital will disarm and disband the moment the war is over, at least not without a political settlement that creates a path for demobilisation.

This is the context in which SAF chief and de facto president General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan’s recently announced national dialogue should be read, less as a comprehensive resolution to the country’s militia problem than as a political process that could convert the army’s wartime alliances into post-war influence.

Burhan has explicitly ruled out the return of RSF leaders to power, promising there would be no “ incomplete peace ” that allowed Hemedti or other RSF leaders back into government. Given the RSF’s abysmal human rights record during the war, the exclusion is defensible, but the broader armed-group problem remains unresolved: namely, how the RSF’s remaining forces would actually be dismantled or integrated, particularly in Darfur, and how the SAF’s own allied militias would be brought under a single chain of command once the shooting slows down.

Another structural problem that is older than this war reinforces why claims of total victory remain elusive. The Sudanese army has long struggled to project sustained power across the country’s peripheries. Under Omar al-Bashir, the government relied on Janjaweed militias to help the army fight the rebellion in Darfur. In 2013, many Janjaweed fighters were brought into the newly created RSF.

There is little reason to think a hollowed-out, cash-poor SAF, dependent on volunteer recruits, Islamist militias and Juba Peace Agreement signatory forces, can now succeed where the pre-war state repeatedly struggled: in Darfur, a region roughly the size of France, where the RSF continues to use cross-border supply routes.

Even if the RSF is somehow eventually broken, its weapons and its fighters will not simply disappear. They will pass to whichever political entrepreneur is best positioned to pick them up. Meanwhile, in Khartoum, the questions of the day after will pry open conflicts that the war has, for now, kept closed.

articles.title: MG Hector Tomahawk launched! Prices, range & more
articles.summary: Electric Vehicles News: JSW MG Motor India has launched the new Hector Tomahawk in India, a new seven-seater SUV that joins the company's line-up. The model has been introduc.
articles.body: JSW MG Motor India has launched the new Hector Tomahawk in India, a new seven-seater SUV that joins the company's line-up. The model has been introduced with both pure-electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains. The Hector Tomahawk EV comes at a starting price of Rs 19.49 lakh, ex-showroom.The Hector Tomahawk EV is also available under the Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS) programme, with prices starting at Rs 13.99 lakh + Rs 4.90/km battery rental. The PHEV BaaS price starts at Rs 21.79 lakh + Rs 3.20/km battery rental, for a limited number of bookings. Hereâs a quick look at all the details you should know. Bookings are now open, with EV deliveries starting in September 2026. PHEV test drives and deliveries will begin in November 2026.MG Hector Tomahawk EV: Details The EV uses a 69.2 kWh battery paired with a permanent magnet synchronous motor producing 150 kW and 310 Nm. It has a claimed 517 km rangeand supports 90 kW DC fast charging. The EV is available in both five- and seven-seat layouts.MG has also equipped the SUV with 18 connected apps, along with what the company describes as India's first Gen AI with karaoke. The SUV measures 4,745 mm in length,1,850 mm in width and 1,770 mm in height, with a 2,810 mm wheelbase. It gets a 15.6-inch HD display for infotaiment, 8.0-inch driver's display, Level 2 ADAS and i-SMART 3.0 with more than 80 connected features.The Hector Tomahawk is the first MG model in India to be based on the company's ADAPT platform, or Advance Drive Architecture Platform Technology. The architecture has been developed to support multiple electrified powertrains, including pure EVs, series hybrids, parallel hybrids and direct-engine-drive configurations.In terms of design, the Hector Tomahawk gets a large and upright SUV profile. MG says the styling draws inspiration from an iconic Allied fighter aircraft used during World War II. The SUV features a long bonnet, high ground clearance, prominent wheel arches and muscular bodywork.At the front, it gets parallel, opposite-facing LED DRLs with rectangular headlamps. The side profile features chunky body cladding and diamond-cut alloy wheels.MG Hector Tomahawk: EV and plug-in hybridThe Hector Tomahawk has been unveiled with both EV and plug-in hybrid powertrain options. The electric version offers a claimed 517 km range, while the plug-in hybrid version gives 115 km of pure electric range. The PHEV combines a 1.5-litre petrol engine, dedicated hybrid transmission and a 20.5 kWh battery. Overall, it offers over 1,100 km range using both a fully charged battery and one full fuel tank. It gets a 148 kW electric motor and can accelerate from 0-100 km/h in around 9 seconds.

articles.title: In the 1940s, a New York handyman began expanding a cabin with railroad ties and cast-off objects; it grew into a seven-storey labyrinth with around 35 caverns and alcoves
articles.summary: US News: Explore the extraordinary story of Clarence Schmidt's House of Mirrors, a unique seven-storey architectural marvel built from discarded materials in Woodstock, NY. Learn about its origins, growth, and artistic significance.
articles.body: Clarence Schmidt did not set out to build one of Americaâs strangest houses. What began as a modest cabin on a wooded mountainside in Woodstock, New York, became an enormous handmade environment of rooms, walkways, balconies, gardens, grottoes and shrines. Built without a conventional architectural plan, the structure expanded as Schmidt found new materials, developed new ideas and reshaped the landscape around him. At its fullest form, the House of Mirrors extended nearly seven storeys down the mountainside and contained roughly 35 caverns and alcoves.According to Philadelphiaâs Magic Gardens, Clarence Schmidt (1897â1978) moved to Woodstock in the 1940s and, having trained as a mason and plasterer, found work as a handyman. His first home, Journeyâs End, began as a simple log cabin made from railroad ties. Schmidt tarred the exterior and covered it with cracked glass, transforming the modest cabin into an unusual reflective structure. The cabin became the starting point for a much larger environment, which Schmidt expanded and altered as he developed the mountainside site.A cabin that kept growingBy the 1940s, Schmidt was reshaping the mountainside around his home. He cleared sections of the steep slope and built retaining walls from locally quarried bluestone, creating terraces that allowed him to work with the terrain. He later built another cabin around a large tree, which became his living quarters and was eventually known as the Inner Sanctum. From there, the project expanded through successive additions rather than according to a fixed architectural plan. Schmidt added rooms, corridors, elevated sections and other structures, connecting them with stairs, galleries, wooden walkways and balconies. The House of Mirrors developed as an interconnected environment that followed the contours of the mountainside rather than the conventions of a traditional house.The landscape continued to shape Schmidtâs approach. Instead of flattening the site to create a conventional building plot, he worked around the existing contours, fitting new sections around structures that were already in place. Walls followed the terrain and terraces stepped across the hillside, while each addition became part of a larger, increasingly complex environment. According to Ricco/Maresca, the House of Mirrors evolved organically as Schmidt continually added and altered elements in response to the landscape. Its windows and reflective surfaces became distinctive features, while the growing structure incorporated roughly 35 alcoves and caverns connected by corridors, galleries and staircases.Where discarded objects became part of the architectureSchmidtâs materials were as unconventional as his approach to construction. Alongside wood and stone, he incorporated mirrors, pieces of glass and objects that had little connection to traditional house building. Discarded items collected from around the area were given new roles within the structure, becoming part of its walls, surfaces and decorative elements. Woodstock Arts notes that Schmidt incorporated a striking assortment of found objects into the House of Mirrors, including car bumpers, wheels, bicycles, lawnmowers, guitars, saw blades, beer cans and doll parts.The result was an immersive environment in which ordinary building materials existed alongside reflections and found objects. Visitors could move through wooden passages and interconnected spaces containing glass, plants and handmade decorations. Some areas resembled grottoes, shrines or outdoor enclosures rather than conventional rooms. This approach placed Schmidt within the tradition of self-taught artists who created what are now known as art environments, works that blurred the boundaries between sculpture, architecture, gardening and everyday life. Rather than simply decorating a house, Schmidt transformed the structure itself into an evolving artwork.A fragile masterpiece that disappearedAs the structure became more elaborate, it also became increasingly fragile. Schmidt relied on improvised construction techniques and unconventional materials, including roofing tar, which he used to attach objects and coverings to parts of the structure. In January 1968, the House of Mirrors was destroyed by fire, leaving photographs and written accounts as the main records of the environment he had created. However, Schmidt continued building after the loss. He began another structure, known as Mark II, but it too was destroyed by fire in 1971. His work nevertheless left a lasting impression on other artists, including Philadelphia artist Isaiah Zagar. As a student at Pratt Institute, Zagar visited Woodstock and encountered Schmidtâs environment, an experience that influenced his ideas about art and later informed the development of Philadelphiaâs Magic Gardens.Schmidt died in 1978, while the House of Mirrors had already disappeared from the mountainside. Its legacy endured as an important example of an art environment created outside conventional architectural and artistic systems. Its significance lay not only in its extraordinary appearance, but also in the way Schmidt transformed an ordinary cabin into an evolving handmade world. He used materials around him, worked with the landscape and continued adding to the structure until architecture, sculpture and the mountainside became closely intertwined.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 47-year-old California pastor makes college football roster 30 years after an injury ended his career, inspired by a video of a 60-year-old player
articles.summary: US News: A 47-year-old California pastor has returned to college football nearly three decades after an injury ended his playing career, after his son showed h.
articles.body: A 47-year-old California pastor has returned to college football nearly three decades after an injury ended his playing career, after his son showed him a video of a 60-year-old man playing the sport. Justin Buzzard, a pastor, husband and father of three, has made the San JosÃ© City College Jaguars roster as a defensive end after spending years away from competitive football. Buzzard played football in high school and continued into college before injuries forced him to stop in the 1990s. Decades later, a video showing an older man playing football prompted his son to ask whether his father could make a similar comeback. Buzzard took the challenge seriously, began training again and eventually contacted San JosÃ© City College. After working through practices and conditioning with players far younger than him, he earned a place on the roster and is now preparing for the 2026 season.How a 47-year-old California pastor returned to college footballBuzzard's return began with a challenge from his son rather than a long-planned attempt to revive his football career. According to Buzzard's account to NBC Bay Area, his son showed him a social-media video featuring a man in his 60s playing football and questioned why his father could not get back on the field. Buzzard initially thought the suggestion was unrealistic, but the idea stayed with him. He eventually contacted San JosÃ© City College and asked about the possibility of joining the football programme. That conversation led to an opportunity to train with the team, where Buzzard had to demonstrate that he could handle the physical demands of college football. He began conditioning and participating in practices during the summer, working towards the same goal as much younger players. The decision represented a return to a sport he had left behind almost 30 years earlier after injuries ended his original playing career.An injury ended his first football career in the 1990sBuzzard already had years of football experience before his unusual comeback. He played four years of high-school football and then spent one year playing at college level, but injuries eventually forced him away from the sport. Nearly three decades later, he has returned to the field as a defensive end for the San JosÃ© City College Jaguars. His age makes the comeback unusual, but his previous experience also means he is not learning football from scratch. The challenge has instead been rebuilding the physical conditioning required to play a demanding contact sport after years away. Buzzard has spoken about wanting to remain healthy while competing alongside players who are young enough to be his children. His return is therefore not simply a symbolic appearance. He has gone through the process of training, practising and earning a place on the roster.He made the roster alongside much younger playersBuzzard's teammates are predominantly traditional college-age athletes, creating an enormous age gap between him and many of the people sharing the field. Reports say some of his teammates are around the age of his oldest son, yet Buzzard has said the players have welcomed him rather than treating him as an outsider. His teammates have reportedly given him the nickname "OG", reflecting his status as the oldest player in the group. San JosÃ© City College coach Jim Winkler told ChurchLeaders that Buzzard was expected to follow the same standards and rules as everyone else on the team. Buzzard has also made clear that he does not want younger players to go easy on him because of his age. His goal is to compete on the field rather than simply serve as an inspirational presence on the sidelines. The fact that he earned a roster place after going through the team's preparation process makes the comeback more significant than simply showing up for a practice.His family had concerns about the physical risksBuzzard's decision to return to contact football also required support from his family. He has been married for more than two decades and has three sons, and his wife initially had reservations about him actually playing in games. Buzzard told Fox News that she was happy for him to make the team but did not initially want him to take part in games because of the potential for injury. Her position later softened, and reports say she now has his games on her calendar and plans to support him. Buzzard has also emphasised the importance of staying healthy as he prepares for the season. The concern is understandable given that injuries were what ended his original football career. His comeback therefore involves a genuine physical risk, particularly because he is returning to a contact sport after a prolonged absence. Nevertheless, Buzzard has continued with the programme and has made clear that he wants to see how far he can take the opportunity.Football is now part of his life alongside his ministryBuzzard's return to the field is taking place alongside his work as a pastor. He is the founder and lead pastor of Garden City Church in the South Bay and has spent years speaking about personal growth, fatherhood, relationships and taking meaningful risks. His football comeback has naturally become connected to that message. Buzzard has described his philosophy with the phrase "risk or rust", arguing that people should continue challenging themselves rather than allowing fear or comfort to prevent them from pursuing meaningful goals. The football experiment gives him a personal example of that philosophy. He is attempting something physically demanding that he had not done for decades while continuing his responsibilities as a pastor, husband and father. His return has therefore become more than a sports story for him. It is also an example of the idea that people can revisit ambitions they once considered finished.His goal is to compete during the 2026 seasonMaking the roster was only the first milestone in Buzzard's comeback. He wants to remain healthy, participate in the season and have an opportunity to contribute on the field. He wears No. 48, a reference to the age he will turn in September. His preparation has involved training alongside much younger athletes, and he has said that he does not expect special treatment because of his age. The San JosÃ© City College Jaguars are preparing for the 2026 season, giving Buzzard the opportunity to turn an unusual comeback story into an actual competitive season. How much playing time he receives remains to be seen, and simply making the roster does not guarantee that he will appear regularly in games. For now, however, he has achieved the part that once seemed almost impossible. A career that ended with injury in the 1990s has been revived nearly three decades later, after a conversation with his son gave him the push to try again.A decades-old football dream has a second chanceBuzzard's story stands out because the comeback was not the result of a professional opportunity or a carefully planned athletic campaign. It began with his son showing him a video of an older football player and asking a simple question. Buzzard could have dismissed the idea because of his age, his previous injuries or the decades that had passed since he last played. Instead, he decided to find out whether a return was possible. He trained, approached a college programme and eventually earned his place alongside players decades younger than him. Whether he becomes a regular contributor during the season remains uncertain, but the achievement has already given him the chance to finish a chapter that was abruptly ended by injury. For Buzzard, the return to football is also an opportunity to demonstrate the message he has encouraged others to follow: an old setback does not necessarily have to determine what comes next.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1917, the Crane family bought the first piece of Choate Island; decades later, the island entered the Crane Wildlife Refuge under the Trustees in 1974
articles.summary: US News: Explore the fascinating transformation of Choate Island from a thriving agricultural landscape to a protected wildlife refuge. Discover its historical significance, diverse ecosystems, and the legacy of the Crane family.
articles.body: For centuries, the island supported Indigenous communities, farms, livestock and family homes before becoming a wildlife refuge on the Massachusetts coast. Choate Island, once known as Hog Island, is now the largest island in the Crane Wildlife Refuge, where salt marsh, grassland and forest frame historic buildings that date back more than two centuries. Its transformation was gradual, beginning with the Crane family's early-20th-century land purchases and ending with MinÃ© Crane's 1974 gift to The Trustees of Reservations.According to The Trustees of Reservations, Choate Island is the largest island in the Crane Wildlife Refuge, covering 135 acres within the refugeâs 697-acre network of coastal islands and marshes in the Essex River Estuary. More than 200 bird species have been recorded across the refuge, while Choate Island provides habitat for mammals including deer, fisher, coyotes and otters. Its spruce forest supports birds such as golden-crowned kinglets and sharp-shinned hawks, while its grasslands provide important habitat for bobolinks and Savannah sparrows.From Indigenous land to a farming islandAccording to Babson Historical Society, Indigenous communities in the region had established agricultural settlements and maintained a mixed subsistence economy based on farming, fishing, hunting and shellfish gathering. The Agawam and other Indigenous communities used the coastal landscape and surrounding estuaries long before the Crane family arrived, while the islands later became part of a farming landscape that remained important through the 18th and 19th centuries.European settlers later called Choate Island âHog Islandâ, reflecting its role in the regionâs colonial farming system. The Choate family became closely associated with the island after Thomas Choate acquired land there in the late 17th century, with subsequent generations developing and maintaining farms for generations. The Choate House, built in the early to mid-18th century, became the centre of the familyâs long presence. Choate Island and neighbouring Long Island were connected by a causeway, allowing people, livestock and agricultural goods to move between them, while fields, grazing areas, stone walls and farm buildings developed alongside salt marshes and tidal waters. The island was officially renamed Choate Island in 1887.The Cranes arriveThe Trustees of Reservations also note that the next major change came in the early 20th century, when Richard T. Crane Jr., the Chicago industrialist who was developing the Crane Estate around Castle Hill, acquired the first portion of Choate Island in 1917. The Crane family expanded its holdings in 1927, bringing more of the island into the estate. Rather than removing every trace of its agricultural past, the Cranes retained historic structures, including the Choate House and the nearby Proctor Barn on Long Island, while reshaping parts of the landscape for their own use.One of the most visible changes was tree planting, with Cornelius Crane establishing about 95 acres of spruce and pine forest on Choate Island in the 1930s. Norway spruce became one of the dominant species, creating a prominent new feature in the islandâs landscape. Over the decades, however, severe storms damaged large sections of the ageing plantation, prompting The Trustees to remove about 30 acres of trees and restore the area as shrubland and young forest habitat. Crane and his wife, MinÃ©, also developed a strong personal connection with the island, using the White Cottage, designed by architect Royal Barry Wills, as a private retreat overlooking Ipswich Bay and the surrounding marshes. The couple were later buried near the islandâs summit, where their graves overlook the landscape that had become an important part of their lives.From private estate to wildlife refugeAccording to Historic Massachusetts, MinÃ© Crane donated about 700 acres of land, including Choate Island and surrounding islands and salt marshes, to The Trustees of Reservations in 1974 in memory of her husband, Cornelius Crane. The gift formed the foundation of the Crane Wildlife Refuge, which was later expanded through additional acquisitions and donations. The transition from private estate to protected refuge did not mean freezing the landscape in its historic state. Instead, conservation work has continued to respond to changing ecological conditions. In 2017, for example, The Trustees and conservation partners cleared about 30 acres of ageing Norway spruce plantation after severe storms had damaged large sections of the forest. The project created space for shrubland and young forest habitat, supporting species including American black ducks, American woodcocks, eastern towhees and native pollinators. This approach reflects a broader conservation goal: maintaining a functioning coastal ecosystem rather than preserving every element of the landscape exactly as the Cranes left it. Today, visitors can follow gravel roads and mown trails past the historic Choate House towards the Crane burial site near the islandâs highest point. The route passes through a changing landscape of grassland, woodland, shoreline and salt marsh, showing how natural habitats and historic features coexist on the island.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Crane Jr., the Chicago industrialist who was developing the Crane Estate around Castle Hill, acquired the first portion of Choate Island in 1917. The Crane family expanded its holdings in 1927, bringing more of the island into the estate. Rather than removing every trace of its agricultural past, the Cranes retained historic structures, including the Choate House and the nearby Proctor Barn on Long Island, while reshaping parts of the landscape for their own use.One of the most visible changes was tree planting, with Cornelius Crane establishing about 95 acres of spruce and pine forest on Choate Island in the 1930s. Norway spruce became one of the dominant species, creating a prominent new feature in the islandâs landscape. Over the decades, however, severe storms damaged large sections of the ageing plantation, prompting The Trustees to remove about 30 acres of trees and restore the area as shrubland and young forest habitat. Crane and his wife, MinÃ©, also developed a strong personal connection with the island, using the White Cottage, designed by architect Royal Barry Wills, as a private retreat overlooking Ipswich Bay and the surrounding marshes. The couple were later buried near the islandâs summit, where their graves overlook the landscape that had become an important part of their lives.From private estate to wildlife refugeAccording to Historic Massachusetts, MinÃ© Crane donated about 700 acres of land, including Choate Island and surrounding islands and salt marshes, to The Trustees of Reservations in 1974 in memory of her husband, Cornelius Crane. The gift formed the foundation of the Crane Wildlife Refuge, which was later expanded through additional acquisitions and donations. The transition from private estate to protected refuge did not mean freezing the landscape in its historic state. Instead, conservation work has continued to respond to changing ecological conditions. In 2017, for example, The Trustees and conservation partners cleared about 30 acres of ageing Norway spruce plantation after severe storms had damaged large sections of the forest. The project created space for shrubland and young forest habitat, supporting species including American black ducks, American woodcocks, eastern towhees and native pollinators. This approach reflects a broader conservation goal: maintaining a functioning coastal ecosystem rather than preserving every element of the landscape exactly as the Cranes left it. Today, visitors can follow gravel roads and mown trails past the historic Choate House towards the Crane burial site near the islandâs highest point. The route passes through a changing landscape of grassland, woodland, shoreline and salt marsh, showing how natural habitats and historic features coexist on the island.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: How a family reunion in China ended in a 3-year prison term for artist Gao Zhen
articles.summary: China News: A family visit to China back in August 2024 ended with a three-year prison sentence for a US-based Chinese artist. Gao Zhen, a member of the artistic .
articles.body: A family visit to China back in August 2024 ended with a three-year prison sentence for a US-based Chinese artist. Gao Zhen, a member of the artistic duo the Gao brothers, was given the prison sentence over a satirical artwork involving statues of Mao Zedong.Gao was sentenced on Tuesday by the Sanhei People's Court in northern Hebei province for âinfringing upon the reputation of heroesâ, according to his wife, Zhao Yaliang. The offence relates to artworks that Chinese authorities consider insulting to revolutionary figures.The sentence brought an abrupt end to hopes that Gao, who has remained in official custody since his arrest, would soon be released and return to his family in the US. Zhao said she had prepared clothes for her husband, expecting that he might be freed.âI felt two years was my limit, and I was really disappointed and sad. I haven't been able to catch my breath,â she said.Gao was arrested while visiting family in China in August 2024, after travelling back from the US, where he and his family had immigrated. He has remained in custody for about two years since then.The case centres on several of Gao's satirical works, including Maoâs Guilt, a 2009 statue depicting Mao Zedong, the founder of modern China, kneeling in repentance. Another is the Miss Mao series, which caricatures Mao with breasts and an exaggerated nose.Gao's supporters say the works predate the law under which he was prosecuted. Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders who has advocated for the artist, said Gao plans to appeal.Yi described the case as âa very clear case of a violation of a personâs freedom of expression.âThe court did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Amnesty International also criticised the conviction, saying the sentence was intended to discourage artists from challenging official narratives. Gao was handed the maximum three-year prison term available under the offence.âThe lengthy pre-trial detention and, ultimately, decision to convict Gao Zhen and sentence him to the maximum three-year prison term under this offence illustrate the authoritiesâ determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression,â said Amnesty's China Director Sarah Brooks.âNo artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history,â she said.The Gao Brothers became internationally known for works examining authoritarianism and censorship. Their art was exhibited in China and abroad during a period of relative openness in the country.That space for political expression has narrowed in recent years, particularly when artists and others have addressed prominent political figures. China passed a law in 2018 banning criticism of the nation's âheroesâ, which authorities have since used in cases involving depictions of revolutionary figures.For Zhao, however, the case remains deeply personal. She said she hopes to be reunited with her husband and return with him to the US. Chinese courts often count time spent in pre-trial detention as time served towards a prison sentence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UN rejects Israel’s threat to expel Gaza residents over kite-flying
articles.summary: UN rights office spokesperson slams Israeli threat of forced evacuations from Gaza communities over kite flying.
articles.body:
The United Nations has condemned Israel's threat to expel Palestinians from areas of the besieged Gaza Strip where kites were being flown by children.

"On the threat of expulsion due to children's kite flying, I hope we can all agree that this is outrageous," UN rights office spokeswoman Ravina Shamdasani told reporters on Tuesday.

Israel warned Hamas on Sunday that it would intensify military operations if kites, drones or balloons continue, saying those responsible would be targeted.

Several kites not carrying incendiary devices were reported to have drifted into southern Israeli communities over the last month. The incidents have evoked memories of incendiary kites and balloons launched from Gaza in 2018, in what Palestinians said was a protest against the Israeli blockade of the enclave.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz, in a joint statement on Sunday, said "Israel warns Hamas that if the launches toward Israel do not cease immediately", Israeli forces "will take action to intensify targeted operations against those responsible". They "will evacuate the population from areas from which kites, drones and balloons are launched", it added.

Gaza's popular committees, coordinating with Hamas authorities, urged parents on Monday to stop children flying kites, saying they were acting "to protect their innocent lives".

"Every summer, my kid, Ahmed, and the kids in the street fly those kites to entertain themselves," Umm Mohammed, a mother in Gaza City, told the Reuters news agency. "But [now] I will not allow him to – not any more."

Basem Naim, a member of Hamas's political bureau, rejected the Israeli warning over the kites.

"Is it conceivable that attempts to appease the war criminal Netanyahu have led them to describe innocent children's activities as armed activities, while Netanyahu continues to kill and destroy daily despite the agreement?"

The dispute comes amid a "ceasefire" in Gaza that has failed to halt Israeli attacks. More than 1,280 Palestinians have been killed since the agreement took effect in October, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health.

articles.title: In the 1960s, Takao Shitoâs family refused to surrender its farm for Japanâs Narita Airport; over 50 years later, a runway still bends around his fields
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore the incredible story of Takao Shito, a farmer who refused to sell his family's land for Narita International Airport, shaping its runway's design in the process. Discover his ongoing battle against urban development and the legacy of resistance.
articles.body: In the fields surrounding Narita International Airport, jets pass overhead every few minutes as they climb toward Tokyo. Down below, a farmer named Takao Shito tends rows of carrots, onions and radishes on land his family had worked for nearly a century by the time the airport dispute began. His father refused to leave the land in the 1960s, helping force planners to route one runway around the farm.The dispute began in 1966, when the Japanese government chose Sanrizuka, a rural area about 40 miles from Tokyo, as the site for a new international airport intended to symbolise the country's postwar progress. Local farmers, including Shito's father, resisted fiercely from the outset, and the standoff eventually escalated into violence. The feature outlet Japan Insides says the Shito family farmed the same plot for nearly a century, growing rice and vegetables and raising livestock before the government claimed the surrounding land in the 1960s.Decades of clashes over the landDemonstrations against the airport grew increasingly bitter through the late 1960s and 1970s, and at least a dozen police officers and protesters died in the confrontations that followed. Authorities eventually took over many properties, and the number of resisting farms gradually shrank as families accepted compensation and moved elsewhere. Narita finally opened in 1978, though continued local opposition meant that it initially operated with only one runway. Shito was reportedly offered a large payment to give up the land, but he refused.Shito has told the BBC that he is not interested in money and simply wants to continue farming, even though his fields are surrounded by airport infrastructure and aircraft noise. When the airport later built a second runway, planners had already bought the surrounding lots from their legal owners, some of whom had rented land to the Shito family for generations. Shito refused to sell his own portion, pointing to protections under Japan's Agricultural Land Act, and the airport ultimately redesigned the runway so that it curves around his fields rather than passing straight through them.A shrinking village inside an airportWhere roughly 28 households once farmed in Shito's village before construction began, only a handful remain today, and Shito is now the last resident still living inside the airport perimeter itself. Today, he reaches his fields through underground tunnels beneath the taxiways, works amid the roar of aircraft and sells his organic produce directly to regular customers in the Tokyo area. He has often said that the soil, cultivated by three generations of his family for nearly a century before the airport dispute, is too good to abandon. The government has so far chosen not to compel the sale of the last occupied plots, wary that doing so would reignite the unrest that once defined the area. Shito, now in his seventies, continues to farm each day with help from volunteers who bring food and supplies, including former student protesters from decades past.His fight has become a symbol of the broader Sanrizuka land dispute, one of modern Japanâs longest-running social movements.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: South Korean president calls for greater police accountability after Jeju missing-person cases
articles.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for greater police accountability after public outrage over the handling of a series of missing-person cases on Jeju island.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for greater police accountability after public outrage over the handling of a series of missing-person cases on Jeju island, as reforms are set to give the force a bigger role in criminal investigations. “Police are likely to wield the greatest power among state institutions,” Lee told a cabinet meeting Tuesday, adding that the public questioned whether the force could bear the responsibility. “Responsibility must be strengthened in proportion to the size of the authority.” Four people reported missing on Jeju were found dead over three days through Monday, authorities said. The cases were unrelated, but two had allegedly been closed by the same officer without confirmation that the missing people were safe. The allegations have prompted police to review all 298 missing-person reports handled by the officer. About 10 are being examined for possible improper closure, media reported. One case involved Jang Mi-ran, a 37-year-old woman whose disappearance became a national controversy after police allegedly closed the case without confirming her safety. Her body was found on Monday, 104 days after she vanished. The other involved a man in his 60s whose family reported him missing again, prompting a renewed search that ended with his body being found. A court detained the officer Tuesday on suspicion of dereliction of duty, falsifying official electronic records and obstructing official duties, the Yonhap news agency reported. The officer denied the charges and said he contacted the missing people, the report said, citing a police official. Jeju police told Reuters they had no separate comment on their handling of the cases, which has fueled safety concerns and criticism on social media. Acting National Police Commissioner Yoo Jae-seong apologized and promised measures to prevent a recurrence. Police have ordered supervisory sign-off on missing-person case closures pending an upgrade to their case management system, Yoo told lawmakers Monday. “We will examine the entire system and make institutional improvements so that this never happens again,” Yoo said, pledging to review all cases handled by the officer. South Korean police received 70,814 reports of missing adults last year, official data showed. More than 70,000 such reports have been filed annually since 2022, though the vast majority were solved within 30 days, police say. The controversy comes after the governing Democratic Party stripped prosecutors of their remaining investigative powers in July, citing a history of abuse. The change, due to take effect in October, leaves police with a greatly expanded investigative role.

articles.title: Nepal flash floods: Heavy casualties feared
articles.summary: The flood in Rasuwa - an area north of Kathmandu bordering Tibet - is feared to have swept away villages.
articles.body:
Heavy casualties are feared after a massive flash flood and mudslide along the Tibet-Nepal border washed away villages and damaged roads and infrastructure.

The flood hit early on Wednesday in Rasuwa, just north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu. It was reportedly caused by excessive snow melting into the Bhote Koshi river that flows from Tibet to Nepal.

Twelve people have been rescued so far, and search operations are under way on both sides of the border, with several areas downstream on high alert.

State media in China, which controls Tibet, say there are significant casualties. Nepalese officials anticipate "huge scale loss" and posted videos showing floodwater crashing through villages.

Roads, communications and power in the region have been disrupted and the authorities say the main road to Kathmandu is closed.

"Our logistics company has seven container trucks there, all staffed by Nepalese employees. We have lost contact with all of them. There is no signal, so we cannot reach anyone," Yee Liang, a Chinese businessman based in Kathmandu, told the BBC.

"As far as I know, there was no warning. There were occasional mudslides and landslides, especially in the rainy season, but this one seems much more serious."

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side is unclear but the BBC spoke to Guan Daoxuan in Sichuan province who said he had lost contact with his wife late on Wednesday morning.

She works for a state-run construction company involved in building roads and bridges in Tibet. Guan said Nepalese authorities had tried to send a helicopter to inspect the area because road access had been cut off, but strong winds were making it difficult for the aircraft to reach the site.

Nepal's disaster management authority called on people living near river banks in vulnerable areas to remain alert and take precautions.

"Work has started to take necessary steps in coordination with the medical team, scouts, and Red Cross," Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post, after holding an emergency meeting to take stock of the situation.

Authorities said 13 officers from the armed police force were missing from two posts in Rasuwa district, and they had not been able to contact dozens of other police officers.

Rasuwa saw deadly flooding last year that killed 18 people after a glacier burst on the Chinese side of the border.

Officials have told the BBC that they believe the scale of Wednesday's disaster exceeds last year's floods.

articles.title: In 2002, Lundy began removing invasive rats; 11 years later, Manx shearwater pairs had risen from 300 to 3,000
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Conservation groups began a campaign to remove invasive rats from Lundy, a rocky island in the Bristol Channel in 2002. Ten years later, surveys found.
articles.body: Conservation groups began a campaign to remove invasive rats from Lundy, a rocky island in the Bristol Channel in 2002. Ten years later, surveys found about 3,000 breeding pairs of Manx shearwaters, up from roughly 300 when the recovery project began. Guillemots were also using breeding sites on cliffs and areas that had previously been accessible to rats. The project was launched because rats were preying on seabird eggs and chicks. Lundy had suitable nesting habitat, but several bird populations had fallen sharply. The removal effort eventually made the island rat-free, and subsequent surveys recorded increases across several seabird species. The same basic problem is being tackled on islands thousands of miles away. In the Marshall Islands, a rat-eradication campaign completed in 2024 was followed by the return of thousands of native seedlings and a colony of about 2,000 sooty terns within a year.Why rats became a problem on LundyRecords cited by the Lundy Bird Observatory say both brown rats and black rats were present, and the animals were known to prey on seabirds, their eggs and young. That mattered particularly for burrow-nesting species, since Manx shearwaters spend much of their lives at sea but return to land to breed, and use underground burrows to raise their chicks. The seabird recovery project brought together Natural England, the RSPB, the National Trust and the Landmark Trust. Its objective was to remove the rats and give nesting seabirds a better chance of reproducing successfully.The eradication operation itself ran from November 2002 to March 2004, with work concentrated during two winters. The timing was chosen because natural food available to rats was lower during winter, increasing the likelihood that they would take the bait. Lundy was later confirmed rat-free, with the island formally declared free of rats in 2006. When RSPB survey teams returned in 2013, they found that the number of breeding Manx shearwater pairs had risen from 300 to 3,000. Puffins had increased from five birds to 80, while razorbills and shags had also recorded gains.Guillemots began using more of the cliffsLundy Bird Observatory records show that guillemots were breeding at the island after the rat eradication, with their numbers rising substantially in later surveys. In 2013, researchers recorded 4,114 individual guillemots at breeding colonies, compared with 3,302 in 2008. The observatory also noted that guillemots had begun appearing at new breeding sites in areas of broken ground close to the grassy slopes. Those locations had previously been relatively accessible to rats.The evidence does not mean every change in the guillemot population can be attributed to rat removal, since food availability and other environmental factors also affect seabird numbers. The observatory describes the role of rat removal as a likely factor rather than the sole explanation. By 2021, the breeding census recorded 6,198 guillemots at Lundy, the highest total in the regular survey record at that point. Breeding was confirmed again in subsequent monitoring. The Manx shearwater population also continued to rise well beyond the 2013 survey. A later RSPB-led census estimated 12,638 apparently occupied nesting sites in 2023, equivalent to more than 25,000 individual birds.A similar result appeared in the Marshall IslandsConservationists were dealing with the same type of problem on Bikar Atoll and Jemo Islet in the Republic of the Marshall Islands more than 7,000 miles from Lundy. In 2024, the Marshall Islands government and conservation partners carried out a campaign to remove invasive rats from the two islands. Island Conservation provided technical support as part of the wider Pacific Regional Invasive Species Management Support Service program.In 2025, conservationists reported a colony of about 2,000 sooty terns on Bikar Atoll, where no such colony had been recorded during the previous monitoring. The birds were feeding hundreds of chicks. Conservation teams counted thousands of native Pisonia grandis seedlings across 60 monitored 12-by-12-meter plots. In 2024, they had found none in those plots. Island Conservation's report also notes that Jemo had traditionally been used by people from nearby Likiep Atoll to gather natural resources. Rats had reduced those resources, including coconut crabs, so the restoration effort was intended to have practical benefits for nearby communities as well as ecological ones.The two projects differ in scale, geography and methods, but their monitoring has produced a similar sequence: remove an introduced predator, then watch what happens to species that had been struggling in its presence. In Lundy, the changes have continued for more than two decades. The island now supports tens of thousands of breeding seabirds, while the Marshall Islands project is only beginning its longer-term monitoring. For both sites, the next challenge is keeping rats from returning and tracking whether the early gains persist.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Two dead and warehouse ablaze in Russia after Ukrainian drone strikes
articles.summary: Two people have been killed in a new wave of Ukrainian drone strikes on targets in Russia, news agency Interfax reported on Wednesday, citing officials. The...
articles.body:
Two people have been killed in a new wave of Ukrainian drone strikes on targets in Russia, news agency Interfax reported on Wednesday, citing officials.

The governor of Russia's Lipetsk region, Igor Artamonov, said a man and a 14-year-old girl were killed after a drone crashed into their house, setting it on fire, according to Interfax.

The Defence Ministry in Moscow said on Wednesday that 426 Ukrainian drones had been intercepted and destroyed overnight.

The capital was also among the targets, while airports in Tambov, Nizhny Novgorod and Yaroslavl temporarily suspended take-offs and landings due to air raid alerts.

In the Tambov region, some 600 kilometres south-east of Moscow, a warehouse belonging to the major Russian online retailer Wildberries was targeted. The drone attack caused a fire at the warehouse in Kotovsk, which spread to 100,000 square metres, the region's governor, Yevgeny Pervyshov, said.

Strikes were also launched at Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014. Three Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles were intercepted over the Black Sea, the Moscow-installed governor of the port city of Sevastopol, Mikhail Razvozhaev, wrote on social media.

articles.title: Spain's 'brown challenge': Kids defecating in pools for likes online
articles.summary: Spain's public swimming pools are being hit by a revolting and unhygienic social media trend in which children and teenagers deliberately defecate in pools s...
articles.body:
Spain's public swimming pools are being hit by a revolting and unhygienic social media trend in which children and teenagers deliberately defecate in pools so they can film the ensuing chaos for views and likes online.

The trend, known as the reto marrón ("brown challenge"), is causing widespread outrage and significant damage at outdoor pools across the country, local media report.

Although fines can reach €20,000, in addition to substantial compensation claims and multi-year bans, Spanish media are reporting new cases almost daily.

There is no central record of incidents at the mostly municipally run pools, but there were around 300 last year and already "hundreds" so far this year, broadcaster Cadena Ser reported.

Catching perpetrators in the act is difficult, however. Some reportedly bring faeces in plastic bags hidden in their swimwear and empty them into the water, the newspaper La Razón reported.

In the northern Spanish city of Burgos, however, fine proceedings have now been launched against the parents of four children aged between 11 and 13, the city administration confirmed to dpa. They were seen by an adult releasing faeces in the El Plantío pool. The man immediately alerted police, who took down the children's details.

The parents now face fines of €3,000 ($3,500) each and compensation claims from the municipality for cleaning and disinfecting the pool. If the water has to be replaced, this can cost several thousand euros. The perpetrators themselves also face multi-year bans.

Burgos mayor Cristina Ayala stressed that proceedings would be pursued "to the very end." She said it was already the sixth such case at the city's outdoor pools this year.

Andrés López, a psychiatrist and coordinator for mental health in the Osuna health district, said in an interview with Cadena Ser that this type of behaviour could stem from emotional problems in a particularly vulnerable group such as teenagers and young adults.

He said they use social media to seek recognition or to combat feelings of loneliness. López stressed that social media have certain addictive mechanisms that encourage a bandwagon effect, leading people to imitate this kind of antisocial behaviour.

articles.title: Australia charges man with trying to pass Ukrainian military intel to Russia
articles.summary: The crime of intentional foreign interference carries a penalty of 20 years' imprisonment in Australia.
articles.body:
Australian police said on Friday that a man has been charged with foreign interference for allegedly seeking to inform Russia about Ukrainian military activities.

The 27-year-old Russian-Australian citizen had "military style" training in Russia and later joined the Ukrainian armed forces, Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett said at a news conference.

"We don't want Australia to become a safe haven for people who are undertaking foreign interference on behalf of other countries," she said.

Police alleged he travelled to Russia for the training in October 2024.

He then returned to Australia, they say, where he "maintained contact" with individuals he believed were linked to Russian intelligence.

Police allege he travelled to Ukraine in 2025 where he enlisted in the country's armed forces and "gained access to information relating to their military personnel, units and locations."

He then "provided, or attempted to provide, information obtained in Ukraine to individuals he believed were acting on behalf of Russian intelligence services," Barrett said.

"It is alleged this conduct created a risk to the safety and security of Ukrainian military personnel."

The crime of intentional foreign interference carries a penalty of 20 years' imprisonment in Australia.

Ukraine has been fighting against Russia's full-scale invasion since it was launched in February 2022.

"We have committed over $1.5 billion (€900 million) to help Ukraine defend itself, including more than $1.3 billion (€700 million) in military support through vital equipment for the battlefield and the training of Ukrainian forces, " Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in February last year .

"Australia has been clear since day one that Russia, and those enabling its illegal invasion, will face consequences."

articles.title: How Dolly Parton became the one thing most Americans could agree on
articles.summary: The cultural icon was one of the rare celebrities adored by Americans of all ages, races and political persuasions.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton was a lot of things - a country musician, a philanthropist, an actress, a storyteller and a businesswoman. One thing she never was, however, was a politician.

But don't think it's because no one asked her. In 1999, during an appearance on the talk show Prime Time Country!, the singer was asked by a young woman in the audience if she would ever run for office.

Dolly demurred, with her characteristic razor-sharp wit. "I think of myself more as a diplomat. That's the kind of people who tell you to go to hell in such a way you look forward to the trip."

It's something she'd had to do many times over a career that spanned decades and genres. With a fanbase that included grandmas and Gen-Zers, Republicans and Democrats, drag queens and evangelicals, Parton was a kind of unicorn in America's polarised society.

"She is the one person who straddles political divides… the so-called culture wars," said Sarah Phillips, who teaches an Anthropology of Dolly Parton course at Indiana University - and still finds it hard to speak about the singer in the past tense. The professor "curled into a ball" in her office and "just sobbed" upon hearing of the death.

A recent poll by YouGov said that Parton's net approval rating was 65% - compared with Barack Obama's 14%, Taylor Swift's 3%, Donald Trump's -19% and Joe Biden's -18%.

Much of that universal appeal has been attributed to Parton's steadfast refusal to weigh into politics, for fear of alienating her fans.

"I've got as many Republican fans as Democrats and I don't want to make any of them mad at me, so I don't play politics," she once said during an interview with Fox News.

She turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom from two different presidents. She twice declined Donald Trump's offer, citing scheduling and health reasons. So when Joe Biden offered it to her a few years later, she felt she had to decline as well, otherwise it would look like she had a preference for one over the other.

Elton John, Oprah Winfrey and Paul McCartney lead tributes to Parton

How Parton told her life story through six iconic songs

After news broke on Tuesday of Parton's death, tributes poured in from politicians from both sides. Trump ordered American flags to be flown at half mast - an honour usually reserved for elite statesmen and judges.

"There has never been anyone like her, and never will," Trump wrote on social media.

In her own social media post, Hillary Clinton wrote "she was the best of America".

Even though she avoided partisan politics, Parton was never apolitical - speaking about subjects including women's rights, LGBTQ equality and Black Lives Matter .

That commitment to speaking her mind, and her "amazing sense of self", Phillips said, was integral to Parton's near-universal appeal and self-styled diplomacy.

"She has always been a model for women, carving your own path, looking out for yourself, making sure that you retain the rights to your intellectual property, looking out for your own financial and creative independence," Phillips told the BBC.

"And if that's not feminism, I don't know what is."

Public interest in Parton's views began many years ago, when she made it clear to anyone listening that she was not a cookie-cutter country singer.

In 1977, she became a crossover pop sensation, but instead of alienating her base, she grew her audience. Then, in 1980, she made her film debut in 9 to 5, a dark satire about women's rights in the workplace helped by Jane Fonda. Fonda was persona non-grata in many parts of the country for her anti-Vietnam War activism.

But Parton refused to distance herself from Fonda just to appease her more conservative fans. She said: "I respect anybody's beliefs and the fact that they're willing to stand up for whatever it is. But I'm also the kind of person that if I don't like where you got it, I can tell you where to put it."

After learning of her death, Fonda posted on social media: "She is woven into all our lives and hearts forever."

Parton's image is similarly woven into public minds: always camp, always glamorous, always smiling and always kind. Her aesthetics were deliberately cultivated, another calculated move from a shrewd entrepreneur who understood showbusiness as well as she understood people.

When television journalist Barbara Walters grilled Parton about her looks in a 1977 segment - asking if the singer was a joke - the interviewer arguably met her match.

"Dolly Parton made it very clear that she knows exactly what she's doing," Phillips said, reflecting on how Parton handled the interview.

"This is how she feels comfortable, and she even said [to Walters]: 'Everybody thinks that the joke's on me, but in fact, the joke is on the public. I know very well what I'm doing, and I can change my image any time I want to.'"

Journalists have tried - and failed - over the years to get Parton to go off script. But whenever they asked her to weigh into political terrain, she would pivot like a boxer.

Instead of left-hooks, Parton's main defences were humour and self-deprecation. During a press conference in 2016, she told a gaggle of journalists that "I've been thinking about running myself… we could use a few more boobs in the race", and nodded at her chest.

But Parton never did run for office - even though her father, when he was alive, liked to drive around town with a bumper sticker that said "Dolly for President".

Instead she poured her heart and soul into her philanthropy - like her Imagination Library, which sent free books to children around the world, or her work helping to fund the Moderna Covid-19 vaccine .

Her charity came from a deeply personal place.

Parton grew up in abject poverty, raised in a one-bedroom log cabin alongside 11 siblings. When her career took off, she employed much of her family in her business endeavours and spread that wealth to the local Tennessee community.

She bought an ownership stake in an existing theme park in 1986 in the mountains where she grew up, and it was rechristened Dollywood: a resort and enterprise that remains the single largest employer in the county.

Tennessee musician James Rogers, president of the board of the American Eagle Foundation - which joined forces with Dollywood for a bald eagle sanctuary - recalled the singer's unrivalled kindness and one-on-one attentiveness.

"She's even sweeter than you realise," he told the BBC, recalling a time decades ago when Parton arrived for a performance and spotted him to the side with his wife and daughter Heather, who was around 10 years old.

Parton "detoured the whole entourage to come around over there to where we were and then she knelt down to talk to Heather for a minute".

"The truth is, she supports everybody," said Phillips, who grew up in the North Carolina mountains "across the holler" from Parton's Appalachian Tennessee.

The professor spends "a lot of time" in her class exploring Parton's politics - or "Dollitics", a phrase coined by the singer's nephew to describe her way of handling thorny subjects.

Phillips added that Parton was emblematic of the very values America was built upon and still holds dear, namely "independence" and "freedom to do what you want".

"When we think about the American Dream in the sort of old-fashioned sense of - If you're talented, if you work really, really, really hard, you can achieve your dreams - she embodied that very much."

Phillips and and the many people who paid tribute to the late singer all noted how singular Parton was.

"This summer, I was in France, and I was in Poland, and I ask people, who's the Polish Dolly Parton? Who's the French Dolly Parton?" Phillips said.

"And nobody has an answer, because there isn't one."

articles.title: How Dolly Parton became the one thing most Americans could agree on
articles.summary: The cultural icon was one of the rare celebrities adored by Americans of all ages, races and political persuasions.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton was a lot of things - a country musician, a philanthropist, an actress, a storyteller and a businesswoman. One thing she never was, however, was a politician.

But don't think it's because no one asked her. In 1999, during an appearance on the talk show Prime Time Country!, the singer was asked by a young woman in the audience if she would ever run for office.

Dolly demurred, with her characteristic razor-sharp wit. "I think of myself more as a diplomat. That's the kind of people who tell you to go to hell in such a way you look forward to the trip."

It's something she'd had to do many times over a career that spanned decades and genres. With a fanbase that included grandmas and Gen-Zers, Republicans and Democrats, drag queens and evangelicals, Parton was a kind of unicorn in America's polarised society.

"She is the one person who straddles political dividesâ¦ the so-called culture wars," said Sarah Phillips, who teaches an Anthropology of Dolly Parton course at Indiana University - and still finds it hard to speak about the singer in the past tense. The professor "curled into a ball" in her office and "just sobbed" upon hearing of the death.

A recent poll by YouGov said that Parton's net approval rating was 65% - compared with Barack Obama's 14%, Taylor Swift's 3%, Donald Trump's -19% and Joe Biden's -18%.

Much of that universal appeal has been attributed to Parton's steadfast refusal to weigh into politics, for fear of alienating her fans.

"I've got as many Republican fans as Democrats and I don't want to make any of them mad at me, so I don't play politics," she once said during an interview with Fox News.

She turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom from two different presidents. She twice declined Donald Trump's offer, citing scheduling and health reasons. So when Joe Biden offered it to her a few years later, she felt she had to decline as well, otherwise it would look like she had a preference for one over the other.
