articles.title: Ohio construction workers found a kitten trapped inside an excavator; now she has her own hard hat and a job working with them
articles.summary: US News: A routine day at a construction site in Barberton, Ohio, turned into an unexpected animal rescue when workers discovered a tiny kitten trapped inside .
articles.body: A routine day at a construction site in Barberton, Ohio, turned into an unexpected animal rescue when workers discovered a tiny kitten trapped inside an excavator. The crew at River Reach Construction heard persistent meowing coming from a Komatsu machine and soon realised that the cries were coming from somewhere inside the heavy equipment. Supervisor Chase Guello investigated and helped free the kitten after removing the excavatorâs skid plate. The tiny rescue was later named Sue and quickly became part of the construction crewâs story. What makes the tale even more adorable is what happened next. Sue was given a tiny high-visibility vest and a miniature hard hat, transforming the rescued kitten into the construction companyâs unofficial mascot.Ohio construction workers find kitten trapped inside an excavatorThe unusual rescue began when workers at River Reach Construction heard a kitten crying from inside one of their excavators. The sound was coming from somewhere within the heavy machinery rather than from around the construction site, prompting supervisor Chase Guello to investigate. He eventually discovered the tiny kitten hiding inside the Komatsu excavator. Workers carefully removed the machineâs skid plate, allowing them to reach the animal and get her out safely. The rescue was filmed and later shared online, where the sight of a tiny kitten emerging from a huge piece of construction equipment quickly captured peopleâs attention. For the workers, however, the priority was simply getting the frightened animal out of the machinery without hurting her.The tiny kitten was named Sue after the rescueOnce the kitten was safely out of the excavator, the workers gave her the name Sue as a playful reference to the Komatsu machine in which she had been found. The crew could not locate her mother following the rescue, so Sue was placed with a foster family where she could receive care while recovering. Although she was no longer living inside the construction machinery, the workers who rescued her continued to follow her progress. What started as an unexpected discovery at a worksite soon developed into a much more heartwarming story, with the crew becoming attached to the tiny kitten they had pulled from the excavator.Sue is set to become the construction companyâs shop catSueâs connection with the construction crew did not end with her rescue. River Reach Construction decided to keep her as part of the companyâs extended family, with plans for her to become the shop cat. Local reporting said she will be cared for by shop mechanic Jared and his family. That means the kitten has effectively gone from an unexpected stowaway inside a piece of heavy machinery to a permanent member of the construction companyâs world. While calling her a worker is clearly playful, Sue now has something resembling an official role at the company, giving the tiny rescue an unusually happy ending.The rescued kitten even received her own hard hatSueâs new status came with some remarkably appropriate accessories. Following the attention generated by her rescue, the kitten received a miniature high-visibility vest and a tiny hard hat. The hard hat was made with openings that allow her ears to fit through, making the little construction outfit even more adorable. Photos of Sue wearing the gear helped turn her into the perfect mascot for a construction company. She may not be capable of operating an excavator or carrying out actual construction work, but she certainly looks the part of the crewâs smallest member.Her rescue story quickly captured attention onlineRiver Reach Construction shared footage and updates about Sue on social media, helping the unusual rescue reach audiences far beyond the Ohio construction site. Viewers were particularly drawn to the contrast between the enormous excavator and the tiny kitten that had somehow ended up inside it. The story also prompted plenty of playful reactions, with people online joking about Sue receiving her own hard hat and effectively becoming the crewâs newest employee. The attention has given the construction workersâ unexpected rescue a life far beyond the original incident and turned Sue into a memorable internet mascot.From excavator stowaway to construction mascotSueâs journey is remarkable because of how quickly her circumstances changed. She went from being a vulnerable kitten trapped inside heavy machinery to receiving care from a foster family and eventually finding a permanent place connected to the construction crew that rescued her. Her tiny safety vest and hard hat are clearly more about fun than function, but they perfectly capture the affection the workers have developed for her. What could have ended as a dangerous incident involving an animal trapped inside an excavator instead became a heartwarming rescue story. Now Sue has a safe future, a family to care for her and perhaps the most unusual job title on the construction site, the crewâs tiny shop cat.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: The wit and wisdom of Dolly Parton: 'If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain'
articles.summary: The much-loved country singer-songwriter in her own words, following her death aged 80.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the much-loved US singer-songwriter who has died at the age of 80 , was known for her pearls of wisdom and humour as well as her music.

She regularly offered her perceptive and witty insights about life, music, fame and equal rights.

Here are some of her most memorable quotes from down the years:

"The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain."

"I always just thought if you see somebody without a smile, give 'em yours!"

"I'm not going to limit myself just because people won't accept the fact that I can do something else."

"If you don't like the road you're walking, start paving another one."

"Don't get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life."

"Sometimes, what would look like to be my biggest mistakes turn out to be my biggest blessings."

"I actually take my songwriting more serious than anything else I do, so I would say I am a songwriter first."

"It's my way of expressing myself. It's my therapy."

"You have to search for a long time because I've written a lot of songs. But yes, there are pieces of me, of course, in everything I write."

"I have to write and sing. See, that was my first love, and I have to do that forever, however I have to do it."

"I look totally artificial, but I am totally real, as a writer, as a professional, as a human being. A rhinestone shines just as good as a diamond."

"My dream was always to make as many people happy as I could in this life."

"I always count my blessings, more than I count my money. I don't work for money, never did. It was the art, it was the job. I loved the work. And I've done well, and I'm thankful for it."

"I wanted more than to just be a farmer's daughter, even though I'm proud to be [one]. I just wanted pretty things. I wanted money to buy the things I had always been impressed with as a child. I wanted, I guess, to be a star."

How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs

Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millions

'I’ll think of you each step of the way' - Taylor Swift leads tributes after Dolly Parton dies aged 80

"If I was trying to describe myself to someone that had never seen me before, I would say, 'Calm down. Don't get scared. It's just me. I know I look totally bizarre and artificial, but I'm totally real inside.'"

"I'm not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I'm not dumb - and I'm not blonde either."

"It costs a lot of money to look this cheap."

"People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don't know, I'm never there."

"If I see something sagging, bagging and dragging, I'm going to nip it, tuck it, and suck it."

"I don't like to be like everybody else. I've often made the statement that I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable. That's the easiest thing in the world to do."

"I make jokes about it, but it's the truth that I kind of patterned my look after the town tramp. I didn't know what she was, just this woman who was blond and piled her hair up, wore high heels and tight skirts, and, boy, she was the prettiest thing I'd ever seen. Momma used to say, 'Aw, she's just trash', and I thought, 'That's what I want to be when I grow up. Trash.'"

"I'm pretty sharp. I'm not educated and I'm not that intelligent, but I'm smart. They say somebody's street smart. I feel like if I got intelligence, it's just a country smart."

Journalist: "What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?" Dolly: "The fact that sometimes my mouth is a little too big and a little too open and sounds too much like a sailor."

"I'm very real where it counts, and that's inside."

"They say love isn't about two people gazing into each other's eyes, it is about two people gazing outwards in the same direction. I believe this with all my heart."

"I never really tried to hide myself from anybody. I think that's one of the reasons I'm still around, people feel like they know me."

"I don't want to be a star if I have no life."

Speaking more about the book gifting programme for children: "Since I had no kids and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom. So I think a big part of my success is the fact that I was free to work. And I didn't have children, because I believe that God didn't mean for me to have kids, so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like the Imagination Library."

"I ain't never gonna be old because I ain't got time to be old. I can't stop long enough to grow old. I'm just gonna be the best I can be at whatever age I am."

"When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best. I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."

"When I die, I'll really be getting to live then because I believe that there is a greater place than this".

Journalist: "What would be her funeral song?" Dolly: "I don't know - but I won't be singing it!"

"Yes, I support gay marriage. They have every right to be as miserable as straight people."

"And of course black lives matter. Do we think our little white asses are the only ones that matter? No!"

"I've got transgender people. I've got gays. I've got lesbians. I've got drunks. I've got drug addicts - all within my own family. I know and love them all, and I do not judge."

"It's a good thing I was born a girl, otherwise I'd be a drag queen."

In a letter to young recipients of books from Dolly Parton's Imagination Library: "You and all of your friends are very special. There is no limit to what you can do or how far you can go."

She continued: "Just remember the lessons my family taught me - dream big dreams; learn everything you can learn; and care for all those who care for you. You do all of these things and you can be anyone you want to be.

"You are terrific, and remember... I will always love you."

Dolly Parton: The life of an iconic country singer

articles.title: Canada's retaliation tests the limit of American power under Trump
articles.summary: The president is using US dominance to challenge allies and enemies alike - but both Canada and Iran have found ways to fight back.
articles.body:
Two days before US-Canada trade talks dramatically derailed, Vice-President JD Vance was telling an audience at a private fundraiser that Prime Minister Mark Carney was a "very sweet guy".

In a private audio recording leaked to the Canadian Press, Vance reportedly went on to say that Carney "comes in and puffs his chest out and says: 'I'm going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.'"

He described that approach as "hilarious" because the Canadians ultimately "climb down on a lot of issues".

Maybe those comments, which received considerable coverage in Canada, were not the proximate cause for Carney's diplomats to pack up and go home over the weekend. But they certainly didn't help.

Carney's move abruptly terminated negotiations over a new trade agreement and sparked a fresh round of tariffs between neighbours who conduct more than $872bn (£640bn) in bilateral annual trade.

The serious and deepening rift - and Vance's comments - offer the latest example of a Trump administration willing to exert force on the global stage against friend and foe alike, again highlighting the potentially disruptive consequences of such actions.

What's more, if Trump thought the Canadians would cave in the face of American pressure - as many US allies have done over the past 19 months - he may have miscalculated. And the consequences of that mistake could linger for the rest of his presidency.

While the latest rupture is striking, friction between the US and Canada dates back to the first Trump administration and the negotiations that created the USMCA: the deal replacing the 1990s-era North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta).

Complicating matters were personal clashes between Trump and Justin Trudeau, who was then Canada's prime minister. As Trump prepared to return to the White House in late 2024, he derisively referred to Trudeau as "governor" and to Canada as America's "51st State."

Underlying those insults was a geopolitical outlook that positioned the US primarily as a hemispheric power entitled to exert political, military, and economic influence over its immediate region – and that most definitely included Canada.

Administration officials viewed Canada as contributing too little to regional defence while disproportionately benefiting from trade with its southern neighbour.

In Trump's worldview, where economic security and national security are inextricably linked, Canada and Mexico - two of America's largest trading partners - became early, obvious targets.

"If you listen to really anybody in state, treasury, or commerce [departments], you will hear the phrase 'economic security is national security'," said Drew Delong, head of corporate statecraft at the Kearney Foresight think tank.

By the start of this year, however, as North American trade negotiations proceeded in fits and starts, Trump's attention shifted away from Canada to his military interventions in Venezuela and then the Middle East.

Across every region, though, the core line of Trump's international strategy remains consistent: the US is a dominant power capable of imposing its will for national benefit.

But power has limits. Trump's second term has been a continuous test of those limits - and, at times, a lesson in finding exactly where they are.

While obvious differences exist between a shooting war in Iran and a trade dispute with Canada, the lessons are not dissimilar. In both, the US faces a counterpart that, despite having far less overall power, retains the means to retaliate.

For Iran, that leverage lies in targeting US allies and disrupting global commerce by threatening maritime chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz.

Canada, for its part, is beginning to test its own ability to inflict economic pain. Tuesday's targeted tariffs mark a first step. Future measures could include restricting US access to Canadian energy and critical minerals, alongside consumer boycotts of American goods.

"As the broader world shifts into a more economic security theatre, you see this game of chokepoints and leverage angles continue to pan out across supply chains," said DeLong. Countries just have to look for them, he added.

For the moment, clear exit ramps are scarce. Trump has escalated his rhetoric, repeatedly accusing Canada of "ripping off" the US, while Ontario Premier Doug Ford fired back by telling the American president to "kiss my ass".

"Every time we push allies and partners away, I think we incentivise them to look for new relationships and new partnerships rather than trying to acquiesce to US demands," said Imran Bayoumi, deputy director of the GeoStrategy Initiative at the Atlantic Council.

Still, room remains for cooler heads to prevail. Canada's new tariffs take effect in two weeks, while the most significant US retaliation - a 50% tariff on Canadian-built vehicles and auto parts - will not kick in until early 2027.

As with any conflict - economic or military - a cycle of escalation can prove difficult to break. However, the multi-month buffer before the next wave of US tariffs gives negotiators space to restart talks. Until Friday night, these had been showing some progress.

A more pressing deadline is November's US midterm elections. Democratic congressional victories could significantly curtail Trump's authority - or unexpected Republican success could embolden him further.

At present, Ottawa seems content to bet on the former outcome, calculating that fear of a midterm blowout in key industrial battlegrounds like Michigan and Ohio will force Trump to back down before ballots are cast.

"I don't think there's the kind of internal political divisions in Canada that maybe the Trump administration would have expected," Bayoumi said. "I think Carney has a lot of political runway to really get a good deal for Canada and not settle for anything less."

There is another possibility that Carney has aired publicly since Trump returned to office, however.

Canada may continue shifting away from the US altogether, charting a course that deliberately widens the distance between the two nations. As Carney noted: "We cannot depend on traditional alliances when the rules of the game have fundamentally changed."

While geographic proximity ensures the two countries will remain intertwined, the deeply integrated economic relationship of recent decades may be coming to an end.

In that respect, Canada presents a contrast with Mexico, which appears to be opting for even closer economic integration with the US. Meanwhile, other global trading partners - including US allies in Europe and Asia - are watching Canada's "elbows up" resistance as a plausible blueprint for future dealings with Trump.

"Ten years from now, this is going to be taught in classrooms," said DeLong. "You have these bifurcating paths within North America, and the question is: Are they going to come back together, or is this going to continue to split? And if it does, who benefits most in the long run?"

If the supposedly easygoing Canadians can stand up to their pugnacious – and powerful - neighbour, others may decide they can, too.

articles.title: Thameslink to replace over 60,000 'ironing board' train seats
articles.summary: Govia Thameslink Railway says these upgrades are part of the wider renationalisation plans.
articles.body:
More than 60,000 seats on Thameslink trains are set to be upgraded as part of plans announced by Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR), less than 100 days after it came under public ownership.

All 115 Thameslink trains will get new seat cushions and backrests, replacing the much-criticised seats dubbed "ironing boards" by passengers.

The work is expected to begin in 2027 and take place over a two-year period.

First-class seats would also receive upgraded seat cushions, while seat-back tables would be installed on the 70 trains that do not currently have them, GTR added.

The seat upgrades are part of wider improvements planned for the Thameslink network after GTR came into public ownership in May 2026 .

Other measures included an increase in Gatwick Express services from December and a programme to refurbish train toilets and remove graffiti across the fleet.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said: "We'll start getting rid of the dreaded 'ironing board seats' so passengers can enjoy comfier, more pleasant journeys on some of Britain's busiest commuter routes."

Alexander said wider rail reforms would continue under the planned Great British Railways organisation, which is intended to oversee rail services across England.

John Whitehurst, chief executive of GTR, said passenger feedback had played a key role in shaping the plans.

"Our customers told us that comfort matters, which was why we'd been working on plans to improve seating on Thameslink services," he said.

Thameslink operates services across the South East, including Sussex, Surrey and some areas of Kent.

articles.title: Darcie Greene: We have to be prepared
articles.summary: The FA WNL Cup Group Stage returns on Thursday, with Leeds United Women marking entrance into the competition with a visit to Yorkshire rivals Halifax Women....
articles.body:
The FA WNL Cup Group Stage returns on Thursday, with Leeds United Women marking entrance into the competition with a visit to Yorkshire rivals Halifax Women.

Ahead of the Group T clash, Whites full-back Darcie Greene spoke to leedsunited.com.

"Feeling very good. We've had two excellent results in the first two games of the season, and we are hoping to carry that momentum into the cup match," Greene began.

"However, we are aware that this is just the beginning of the season, and it will only get harder, so we have to be prepared.

"We know Halifax are going to be a tough opponent. We know they've recruited well and will be looking to win the game. We've just got to carry the momentum from the last two victories and compete for another win."

The left-back secured an assist double on Sunday as Leeds ran out 3-0 victors in the FA WNL Division One North clash with Chester-le-Street Town Ladies.

On the attacking side of her game, Darcie added: "Very pleased. I will always look back on my performance and see where I can improve, but being able to contribute to the team in any way is fantastic.

"We know the league is the most important but we obviously want to try to win every game, including the cup matches, and progress as far as we possibly can."

articles.title: Preview: Halifax Women vs Leeds United Women
articles.summary: Leeds United Women begin their FA WNL Cup campaign with a visit to rivals Halifax Women in Group T on Thursday evening.The two sides meet in the cup for the...
articles.body:
Leeds United Women begin their FA WNL Cup campaign with a visit to rivals Halifax Women in Group T on Thursday evening.

The two sides meet in the cup for the second season running, after a 1-0 win for the Whites at Garforth last term where Darcie Greene's incredible solo goal proved the difference.

Last time out for Leeds was a convincing 3-0 win on the road at Chester-le-Street Town Ladies with Amy Woodruff netting a hattrick to guarantee the three points and take home the match ball.

The centre-forward had the Whites in the driving seat at the break after converting instinctively from Darcie Greene's mazy run down the left flank, before bagging two more in the closing stages of the match - another Greene cross tap-in and a glancing header.

The hosts are coming into the clash off the back of a 4-2 win over Norton and Stockton Ancients on home turf, having three first half goals complimented by a stoppage time fourth.

Halifax have won and lost once so far this campaign, placing them in fifth, whereas the Whites are sat joint top of the table having won both games, scoring ten and conceding zero times in the opening two fixtures.

Leeds have pedigree in the competition having lifted the FA WNL Plate back in 2023 in Solihull, defeating Stourbridge Women 3-1, Woodruff getting on the scoresheet.

Action from Myra Shay gets underway at 7.45pm.

Darcie Greene previewed the clash, telling leedsunited.com: "Feeling very good. We've had two excellent results in the first two games of the season, and we are hoping to carry that momentum into the cup match.

articles.title: ENG vs PAK 2nd Test session timings: Start times, lunch and tea breaks for Pakistan tour of England at Lord's
articles.summary: Check complete session timings for the ENG vs PAK 2nd Test at Lord's, including daily start times, lunch intervals, tea breaks, and stumps schedule.
articles.body:
ENG vs PAK 2nd Test session timings: Start times, lunch and tea breaks for Pakistan tour of England at Lord's originally appeared on Cricket News . Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here .

England start as favourites for the second Test at Lord's, having already wrapped up the series opener in three days.

Lord's pitch likely to help the quicks; worry for Pakistan batters.

The Test begins at 11:00 AM local time, with staggered timings for lunch, tea, and stumps across time zones.

ENG vs PAK 2nd Test at Lord's has valuable WTC points on the line

England head into the second Test of their three-match series against Pakistan as clear favourites, with the action getting underway at Lord's on Thursday.

The hosts made light work of the opening Test, wrapping it up inside just three days. Given Lord's own recent reputation for producing bowler-friendly conditions, there's every chance this next match could follow a similarly quick pattern.

England haven't lost any of their last five home Tests against Pakistan, and if the pacers do find some lateral movement with the new ball, then Pakistan could be in trouble again.

When England hosted New Zealand earlier this summer at the same venue, the pitch produced significant lateral seam movement paired with unpredictable bounce.

Those conditions that troubled both teams, and given how badly Pakistan's batters struggled at Headingley in the series opener, it's hard to see them finding much more comfort against a similarly testing surface at the Home of Cricket.

MORE: Joe Root's first reaction to Brydon Carse nightclub handcuff incident ahead of ENG vs PAK 2nd Test

ENG vs PAK 2nd Test at Lord's: Session timings

The second Test match between England and Pakistan begins at 11:00 a.m. local time (BST in London), with staggered breaks across three sessions.

Note: Up to 30 extra minutes may be added daily to complete the required overs.

MORE: ENG vs PAK 2nd Test predicted XI: Babar Azam remains doubtful

How does a typical day of Test cricket break down?

A standard day of Test cricket usually consists of 90 overs, spread across three sessions of roughly two hours each. If time gets lost to weather interruptions during the day, extra playing time can be added afterwards to make up the shortfall.

MORE: Australia vs England for Mike Hussey: Ashes rivals ready to battle it out to secure CSK coach's service

How long do the lunch and tea intervals last?

The lunch break runs for 40 minutes and marks the first significant pause of the day, giving players a chance to rest and reset before the next session gets underway. The tea interval, meanwhile, lasts 20 minutes in a standard Test, though its placement shifts in day-night pink-ball fixtures, where it becomes the first break of the day rather than the second.

articles.title: In 1945, brothers Alfred and Andrew Collier donated 146 Oregon acres to the state as a memorial to their parents; today, Collier Memorial State Park spans 536 acres and preserves the regionâs logging history
articles.summary: US News: Explore the rich history of Collier Memorial State Park, a tribute to the Collier brothers' parents, showcasing over 150 years of logging heritage and serving 350,000 annual visitors in Oregon.
articles.body: In 1945, brothers Alfred D. and Andrew Collier of Klamath Falls donated 146 acres of what would become Collier Memorial State Park to the state of Oregon as a memorial to their parents, Charles Morse Collier and Janet McCormack Collier. The initial 146 acres were only the beginning: over the next four decades, Oregon slowly acquired additional land, thus expanding the park to its present 536 acres. Today, the Oregon Parks and Recreation Department says that the park serves more than 350,000 visitors every year, combining outdoor recreation with one of the countryâs notable collections of historic logging equipment.A family memorial turns into a state parkThe Collier familyâs connection with the property went beyond the memorial donation. The brothers, Alfred D. and Andrew Collier, were involved with Klamath Falls business interests, including the Swan Lake Moulding Company, and their ventures left them with a significant collection of antique logging and lumbering equipment. According to Oregon State Parks, the idea of a logging museum was conceived by the brothers from the beginning, making the preservation of the regionâs timber history part of the parkâs purpose from its early years.In 1947, the brothers donated the first machines that would eventually become part of the Collier Logging Museum. Notably, the collection did not stay limited to those original pieces: donations continued over subsequent decades, while Alfred Collier reportedly continued finding new equipment for the museum until his death in 1988. Through these continuous acquisitions, the collection grew to encompass nearly 150 years of industrial timber history, chronicling the evolution of logging technology from the late 19th century onward.While the outdoor logging museum currently covers an expansive 146-acre footprint, matching the exact total acreage of the brothers' initial 1945 deed, the surrounding park footprint did not remain static. Instead, the state strategically acquired adjacent timber tracts over the years, absorbing the museum into a much larger 536-acre recreational ecosystem.The parkâs expansion from 146 acres to 536 acresThe park expanded over decades rather than in a single acquisition, with the Collier brothers helping acquire additional land through 1962, according to Oregon State Parks. In 1981, the final tract was obtained from the US Forest Service, completing the major additions that brought the park to its current size.Furthermore, the parkâs location helped shape what it became, with the Williamson River and Spring Creek converging within the property and the surrounding landscape connecting the park with broader forests and recreational areas of south-central Oregon. The Williamson River is regionally known for its trout fishery, while Spring Creek is a clear spring-fed stream flowing through the park. Today, visitors can camp, fish, explore trails and visit the outdoor logging museum.Meanwhile, the logging museum remains the parkâs defining historical feature, and its outdoor collection includes rare and antique equipment dating to the 1880s, alongside machinery from later periods. The exhibit underscores how timber harvesting changed as railroads, engines and mechanised equipment transformed the industry. Additionally, the museum contains a cabin village made up of buildings constructed between 1880 and 1920, which were originally sourced from a 100-mile radius across the pine-forested high plains of south-central and eastern Oregon and relocated to the park grounds.Transformation from private tribute to major public destinationThe state organisation reported that donations for the museum continued to grow long after the brothersâ initial contributions. They noted that donations for the museum continued to grow long after the brothersâ initial contributions, rolling in over nearly eight decades to establish a highly comprehensive regional archive.The park itself survived several changes that significantly affected its historic landscape, including the Two Four Two wildfire in September 2020 that burned through part of Collier Memorial State Park and damaged portions of the logging museum. The stateâs Park and Recreation agency reported that most of the museumâs roughly 10,000 artefacts survived, although two major pieces of historic equipment, one of its buildings and areas of the surrounding ponderosa-pine forest were damaged. Despite those changes, the original purpose of the property remains visible through the state-initiated intensive multi-year ecological restoration projects, hazardous tree mitigation, and historical structure rebuilds following the disaster. Thanks to these comprehensive recovery efforts, the park successfully reopened its gates in phases.Today, the parcel given to the state as a family memorial has become a public park that attracts hundreds of thousands of visitors annually, according to the state brochure. Within it, the museum preserves the history of the stateâs logging industry, while Williamson River, Spring Creek, the forest and the campground support recreation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Chantelle Cameron vs Mikaela Mayer: Start time, undercard and how to watch fight this weekend
articles.summary: The pair will top a UK vs US card, with three world titles on the line when they clash in Birmingham
articles.body:
This weekend, Chantelle Cameron and Mikaela Mayer will meet in a title-unification clash, as the pair top a women's UK vs US card in Birmingham .

Cameron puts her WBO super-welterweight title on the line against American Mayer, who holds the WBC and WBA belts , in a meeting of multiple-division champions.

Caroline Dubois is also in action, putting her unified lightweight titles on the line against Amelia Moore, while Terri Harper and Shannon Courtenay are among the other established names competing.

With the legendary Katie Taylor about to retire , her former rival Cameron and Mayer could be vying for the status of boxing's top female star.

When is the fight and how can I watch it?

Cameron vs Mayer will take place at BP Pulse LIVE arena in Birmingham on Saturday 29 August. The main card will begin at 7pm BST (11am PT / 1pm CT / 2pm ET), with main-event ring walks any time from 9.30pm BST (1.30pm PT / 3.30pm CT / 4.30pm ET). The action will stream live on Sky Sports.

articles.title: New York Giants trade Joshua Ezeudu to Chiefs for 2028 draft pick
articles.summary: The New York Giants have traded OL Joshua Ezeudu to the Kansas City Chiefs for a 2028 draft pick.
articles.body:
The New York Giants traded offensive lineman Joshua Ezeudu to the Kansas City Chiefs on Tuesday in exchange for a 2028 seventh-round pick, reports NFL Network's Ian Rapoport . The deal came just before New York 's final preseason game against the New York Jets .

Ezeudu suffered a leg injury in the Giants' 26-3 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 2 of the preseason. The 26-year-old was listed as day-to-day before being traded to Kansas City.

The Giants selected Ezeudu with the No. 67 overall pick in the 2022 NFL draft. He played in all 17 games and started three for New York in 2024. Ezeudu missed all of last season with a calf injury.

The Giants now have another draft pick two years down the line as they continue to shape the roster with younger talent. This is the second future selection New York has acquired recently, after the team received a 2027 sixth-round pick from the Jacksonville Jaguars in exchange for Daniel Faalele .

articles.title: Coke Zero Sugar 400 rain update: Weather forecast for NASCAR race at Daytona
articles.summary: Yes, NASCAR drivers pay close attention to the weather forecast before races at Daytona International Speedway, too.
articles.body:
Daniel Suarez pays attention to the weather forecast before each of his NASCAR races . The upcoming Coke Zero Sugar 400 is no different in that regard.

"Daytona is just very unpredictable because it's so close to the beach that it just changes so much," Suarez told the News-Journal.

A chance of rain and thunderstorms looms for Saturday's big showcase. The Cup Series will hit the track at 7:30 p.m. for its regular-season finale — as long as Mother Nature cooperates.

"It's interesting," said Suarez, who drives the No. 7 of Spire Motorsports. "You never know how it's going to work. That's one of those things we just can't control, and we just hope that things work out good for us."

Here's the latest National Weather Service forecast for this week, as of early Wednesday morning.

National Weather Service forecast for Daytona race week

Wednesday: Showers and thunderstorms likely, mainly after 5 p.m. Mostly sunny, with a high near 91. Light and variable wind becoming east 5 to 10 mph in the afternoon. Chance of precipitation is 60%. New rainfall amounts between a tenth and quarter of an inch, except higher amounts possible in thunderstorms.

Wednesday night: A chance of showers and thunderstorms before 11 p.m., then a slight chance of showers between 11 p.m. and midnight. Partly cloudy, with a low around 73. South southeast wind around 5 mph becoming calm in the evening. Chance of precipitation is 30%.

Thursday: Showers and thunderstorms likely, mainly before 4 p.m. Sunny, with a high near 90. Light and variable wind becoming southeast 5 to 10 mph in the afternoon. Chance of precipitation is 60%.

Thursday night: Showers and thunderstorms likely before 11 p.m., then a chance of showers between 11 p.m. and 2 a.m. Partly cloudy, with a low around 74. South southeast wind around 5 mph becoming calm in the evening. Chance of precipitation is 60%.

Friday: Showers and thunderstorms likely after 2 p.m. Mostly sunny, with a high near 90. Light and variable wind becoming southeast 5 to 10 mph in the afternoon. Chance of precipitation is 60%.

Friday night: Showers and thunderstorms likely, mainly before 8 p.m. Partly cloudy, with a low around 75. Southeast wind around 5 mph becoming calm in the evening. Chance of precipitation is 60%.

Saturday: A 50% chance of showers and thunderstorms after 2 p.m. Mostly sunny, with a high near 89. Light and variable wind becoming east 5 to 10 mph in the afternoon.

Saturday night: A chance of showers and thunderstorms before 2 a.m., then a slight chance of showers. Partly cloudy, with a low around 76. East wind around 5 mph becoming calm in the evening. Chance of precipitation is 30%.

Sunday: A slight chance of showers, then a chance of showers and thunderstorms after 8 a.m. Mostly sunny, with a high near 88. Light east wind increasing to 5 to 10 mph in the morning. Chance of precipitation is 40%.

Sunday night: A 20% chance of showers. Partly cloudy, with a low around 76. East wind around 5 mph becoming calm.

NASCAR schedule for Coke Zero Sugar 400 at Daytona

10 a.m.-noon: O'Reilly Series haulers enter Speedway

8-10 a.m.: Cup Series haulers enter Speedway

7:30 p.m.: O'Reilly Series race — Winn-Dixie 250

7:30 p.m.: Cup Series race — Coke Zero Sugar 400
